text: Arachne’s Weaving: When the Judge Is the One the Work Criticizes
Arachne’s skill at weaving had no illustrious pedigree.
She came from an ordinary family, yet wove wool so exquisitely that people traveled from far and wide to watch her work. Some said such skill must have come from Minerva’s teaching.
Arachne would not accept that.
She said that if Minerva really was better, she should come and compete.
Minerva first appeared as an old woman and urged her to withdraw the challenge. Arachne still refused to yield. The goddess then revealed herself, and each set up a loom.
The contest began.
Minerva wove the order of the gods.

At the center she placed her contest with the sea god for Athens; in the four corners, stories of mortals punished for challenging gods. The whole work displayed not only skill but also who was entitled to determine the world’s hierarchy.
Arachne, however, wove a different set of stories about the gods.

In her images the gods kept changing shape, approaching mortal women as a bull, a swan, a shower of gold, and in other disguises. Rather than place them at the glorious center, she wove the ways they used power, status, and deception into one great cloth.
The two tapestries did not tell of the same world.
Minerva’s work said: those who challenge authority will be punished.
Arachne’s work asked: how do those who hold authority use their power?
After examining it, Minerva could find no fault with its craftsmanship.
Then she tore Arachne’s tapestry apart and struck her with the shuttle in her hand.
Unable to judge the work a failure, the judge simply made it disappear.
On the surface, this contest was entirely fair.
Both practiced the same craft, and both had a full opportunity to display their work. Arachne was not barred from competing. She actually got to place her work before authority.
But whether an evaluation is genuine does not depend only on whether someone has an opportunity to speak.
It also depends on whether, once they have spoken, the evaluator remains bound by the rules of evaluation.
If the judge can destroy an excellent work because its content gives offense, “you may take part” preserves only the outward form of a procedure.
Arachne was allowed to speak.
But what she said was not allowed to have consequences for the judgment.
This is a very common form of sham openness.
Power is willing to hear dissent, provided dissent ultimately proves that power was right all along.
Criticism is permitted, provided it stays within limits that leave everyone’s position unchanged.
People are invited to submit to evaluation, but when the result is unfavorable, the question changes from “How good is the work?” to “Who are you to speak to me like that?”
Minerva did not identify a single misplaced thread.
Instead, she dealt with the person who made it impossible for her to remain comfortably in the judge’s seat.
But Arachne was not a humble, innocent person without any faults.
She publicly boasted of her ability, refused to acknowledge that Minerva might have a connection to the weaving tradition, and answered the contest with a deliberately provocative subject.
All of this deserves judgment.
Being in a weaker position does not automatically make someone right; nor does a work become truthful simply because the power it criticizes is mighty.
The point is that Arachne’s arrogance and the excellence of her weaving are two different matters.
Her understanding of where her craft came from might be narrow, and her work might still be flawless.
Her manner of expression might be deliberately offensive, and the things her work points out might still require an answer.
Her bad attitude cannot simply become a defect in the work’s craftsmanship.
When power conflates these questions, evaluation loses its boundaries.
“You don’t respect me” becomes the answer to “Is what you say true?”
“The way you speak is wrong” becomes a way of avoiding “Did I do what you say I did?”
“Why are you so conceited?” takes the place of “Can I find an error in the work?”
The author’s entire bearing then becomes a reason not to answer the content of the work at all.
This is not merely unfair to the author.
It also deprives power of the chance to learn where it might be wrong.
Minerva herself was also a great weaver.
The story does not portray her as an incompetent figure who suppresses genius through status alone.
That makes the conflict sharper.
The real danger is not an incompetent person occasionally coming to power.
It is someone with genuine ability, experience, and traditional standing beginning to treat their own achievements as the final measure.
She knows how to judge a tapestry.
But once a work brings the very order she belongs to under judgment, she is no longer merely an expert in the craft.
She is also the person being criticized.
These two positions need to be separated.
Someone may be qualified to assess craftsmanship without being suited to decide, alone, the merits of criticism directed at themselves.
The more capable they are, the more readily they may believe they can remain impartial. Yet confidence alone cannot remove the influence of personal interests on judgment.
A genuinely reliable evaluation does not require a judge to have no feelings.
It requires that even an offended judge cannot change the question on that account.
Where does the work fail to hold up?
Which facts are wrong?
What has the argument left out?
If these questions cannot be answered, power cannot punish the author and pretend it has answered them.
The subjects of the two tapestries cannot be passed over either.
Minerva did not simply weave a beautiful design.
She wove the punishment of challengers into its four corners, as if the outcome were already part of the work before the contest began.
Nor did Arachne simply display technique.
She chose stories of gods approaching mortals through disguise and power, making her work a public display of how divine authority was used.
So this contest was never merely an aesthetic comparison.
It was also about who had the right to tell stories about the gods.
Authority usually controls not only the power to act but also how actions are described.
The same transformation can be told as a divine miracle or as a means of concealing an identity.
The same approach can be written as love or as power making refusal impossible.
Arachne’s real challenge may not have been merely “I weave as well as you.”
She was also saying:
You cannot monopolize the interpretation of your own actions.
This was harder for Minerva to tolerate than a contest of skill.
For acknowledging the excellence of the work would only make Arachne a formidable weaver.
Acknowledging that its content required an answer, however, might unsettle how the gods understood their own power.
Yet exposing power does not place someone beyond scrutiny either.
Which stories Arachne selected, how she arranged them, and what competitive intentions she brought to them could still be questioned.
A critic may choose only the material most likely to prove their own answer, or compress complex relationships into a single accusation.
Being in a weaker position does not make someone incapable of error.
A genuine evaluation must therefore reject two simplistic judgments at once:
Authority is being criticized, so the critic must be wrong.
The critic is being suppressed by authority, so the criticism must be right.
The work must be examined as a work.
Power’s response must also be examined as power’s response.
Arachne’s weaving can be questioned.
But questioning must identify where the tapestry misrepresents things, rather than tear it apart and declare that the problem has vanished.
After Minerva destroyed the work and struck Arachne, Arachne hanged herself.
Minerva then let her go on living, but turned her into a spider and commanded her and her descendants to weave webs forever.
This is not a straightforwardly merciful ending.
She preserved Arachne’s ability to weave, but changed the form in which that ability existed.
Arachne still wove, but no longer with her original body, works, and public position.
Power did not eliminate her ability entirely.
It left that ability in a position from which it would no longer compete openly with power itself.
This is more complex even than outright prohibition.
Sometimes an institution does not require a capable person to stop producing.
It only requires that they no longer decide what their work says, or bring it to places where it could influence collective judgment.
The ability can still be put to use.
But the speaker is rearranged into a safe form.
Arachne’s story does not tell us that all authority is untrustworthy, nor does it exempt anyone talented from humility.
The boundary it leaves us is more specific.
A judge may criticize a challenger’s arrogance.
May point out errors in the work.
May uphold the rules of competition, and refuse to treat provocation as a virtue.
But if, unable to find a flaw in the work, the judge turns to destroying the work and its author, this is no longer judgment.
It is simply the exercise of a power that should, for the moment, have been placed behind the rules.
The truly difficult moment in an evaluation is not when the judge faces an obviously failed work.
It is when the work gets something right that the judge is unwilling to admit.
Whether authority is still willing, at that moment, to answer the work rather than deal with its author determines whether the contest was genuine from the start.
Minerva won ultimate control.
But she did not win the argument through her weaving.
After being turned into a spider, Arachne went on weaving webs.
Perhaps this is where the story cuts deepest:
Power can tear up a work, change its author’s position, even decide the form in which she will go on existing.
None of those actions can prove that the work was wrongly woven in the first place.

*Textual basis: the Arachne and Minerva episode in Book 6 of Ovid’s Metamorphoses. This essay follows the continuous account in which Arachne challenges Minerva; their two tapestries display, respectively, divine authority and the gods’ deceptions; Minerva finds no fault in Arachne’s craftsmanship, then destroys the tapestry and strikes her; and finally turns her into a spider. It retains Arachne’s arrogance rather than turning her into a modern heroine of dissent without complexities.*
